problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5y=20{e}^{4x}.
$$
worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5y=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +5=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +5 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+5 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm \text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{c}(x) & ={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $20{e}^{4x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $4$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{4x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=4\alpha {e}^{4x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=16\alpha {e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}16\alpha {e}^{4x}-4(4\alpha {e}^{4x})+5(\alpha {e}^{4x}) & =20{e}^{4x} \\ (16-16+5)\alpha {e}^{4x} & =20{e}^{4x} \\ 5\alpha {e}^{4x} & =20{e}^{4x} \\ 5\alpha  & =20 \\ \alpha  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=4{e}^{4x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+4{e}^{4x}.
$$
